title: What Determines Women’s Employment in Urban Slums?
text:
Introduction


Motivation


Women’s employment is a key indicator of empowerment and household welfare
Urban slum women face multiple barriers — family structure, marital status, and social norms
Very few studies focus on determinants of employment among slum women in India
This study uses data from four urban slums — Atal Ayub Nagar, Nawab Colony, J.P Nagar, Arif Nagar



Research Question

“What determines women’s employment in urban slums — role of marital status, family structure, and age?”



Dependent: Currently Working (Yes/No)
Independent: Marital Status, Family Type, Age
Controls: Education, In-laws Alive

title: What Determines Women’s Employment in Urban Slums?
text:
Data Cleaning


Data collected from four urban slums in 2026
Age = 0 replaced with NA  — data entry error
Education > 16 replaced with NA  — beyond questionnaire range
Marital status recoded: Widowed / Separated = 1, others = 0
Education grouped into six categories: Illiterate, Primary, Middle, Secondary, Higher Secondary, Graduate & Above
Age grouped into six categories: 18–24, 25–34, 35–44, 45–54, 55–64, 65+
Binary dummies created for each education and age category

Key Findings


📊 Marital Status

Married → 14.2% working
Unmarried → 25.0% working
Widowed / Separated → 41.7% working
Economic necessity drives work after loss of spouse




🏠 Family Structure

Nuclear family → 20.1% working
Joint family → 13.4% working
Joint families restrict women’s mobility and work decisions




📅 Age & Education

Women aged 35–44 have highest employment (24.7%)
More educated women work less — social restrictions in slum communities

  geom_smooth(aes(x = INCOMEPC, y = COPC, color = "Given Per Capita Income"),

  geom_smooth(aes(x = income_pc_constructed, y = COPC, color = "Constructed Per Capita Income"),

The confidence interval gives us an idea of the uncertainty around the smooth line, it shows us the range of values within which we can be confident that the true relationship between the two variables lies. THE SMOOTH LINE SHOWS US THE TREND OF THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN EDUCATION AND CONSUMPTION, IF THE LINE IS UPWARD SLOPING THEN IT MEANS THAT THERE IS A POSITIVE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN EDUCATION AND CONSUMPTION, IF IT IS DOWNWARD SLOPING THEN IT MEANS THAT THERE IS A NEGATIVE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN EDUCATION AND CONSUMPTION. THE COLOR OF THE LINE SHOWS US THE DIFFERENCE IN THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN EDUCATION AND CONSUMPTION FOR LAND OWNERS AND NON-LAND OWNERS. text:
When poor families send their children to school, does this help them earn more money and get better jobs in the future? Or do things like caste, where they live, and family background stop them from moving up even with education? Why This Matters Today (in India):
India spends billions of rupees on education ( including different programmes, and sround 4 to 5 percent of the GDP on education) to help people get better jobs and improve their lives.

Some people escape poverty through education, others don’t
The question: Is education really powerful enough to overcome caste, location, and family disadvantage?

title: Does Education Help Poor Families Escape Poverty?
text:
VARIABLES TO EXTRACT:

1. FATHER_EDUCATION_YEARS

From: Income & Social Capital Questionnaire, Section 1
Question: 1.18c
Code: ID18c
Values: 0-16 (years of schooling)




2. HH_CONSUMPTION_ANNUAL

From: Income & Social Capital Questionnaire, Section 14
Questions: 14.1 to 14.52 (ALL items)
Code: CO1 through CO52
How to calculate: Sum all CO items, multiply by 12 for annual
Values: Rupees (₹20,000 to ₹500,000 typical)




3. CHILD_EDUCATION_YEARS

From: Education & Health Questionnaire, Section 11
Question: 11.5-11.6
Code: ED5
Values: 0-16 (years of schooling)
Filter: Child age ≥ 15




4. ANNUAL_INCOME

From: Income & Social Capital Questionnaire, Section 7
Questions: 7.6-7.15
Codes: WS6 (days), WS9 (type), WS10 (rate)
How to calculate:

If WS9=1 (per day): WS10 × WS6
If WS9=2 (per month): WS10 × 12
If WS9=3 (fixed): WS10

Values: Rupees (₹0 to ₹500,000+)




5. OCCUPATION_CATEGORY

From: Income & Social Capital Questionnaire, Section 7
Question: 7.2-7.5
Code: WS3
Categorize as:

1 = Unskilled (codes 03, 04)
2 = Skilled (codes 05, 06)
3 = Professional (codes 07, 08, 09)





6. CASTE

From: Income & Social Capital Questionnaire, Section 1
Question: 1.13
Code: ID13
Values:

1 = Brahmin
2 = Forward/General
3 = OBC
4 = SC (marginalized)
5 = ST (marginalized)
6 = Others





7. RURAL_URBAN

From: Income & Social Capital Questionnaire, Section 1
Question: 1.8
Code: ID8
Values: 0 = Rural, 1 = Urban




8. GENDER

From: Household Roster, Section 2
Question: 2.1
Code: RO1
Values: 1 = Male, 2 = Female

text:

To link father to child: 1. Father ID = RO9 (from Section 2, same questionnaire) 2. If RO9 = 01-12: Father is in household 3. Match father number to ED5 in Education questionnaire 4. Extract father’s education from that row
